Research Project: You will engage in research utilizing advanced analytical chemistry techniques to investigate off-flavor compounds in water and food systems. With mentor guidance, you will learn how to develop optimized sample preparation workflows and instrumental quantification methods to enhance analytical capabilities within the Food Processing and Sensory Quality (FPSQ) Research Unit. Training will include solid-phase microextraction (SPME and SPME Arrow) techniques, GC-MS method development, calibration strategies, and data analysis for semi-volatile compounds.

You will be a part of a collaborative research program focused on understanding the dynamics of off-flavors in salmonid aquaculture and related food matrices. Results generated through this project will be communicated to the scientific community through conference presentations and peer-reviewed publications

Learning Objectives: This experience will provide hands-on learning in multidisciplinary team environments and exposure to real-world research challenges in food quality and chemistry. You will develop competencies in advanced sample-preparation workflows, SPME/Arrow extraction, GC–MS quantification, calibration modeling, and data analysis for semi-volatile compounds

Under the guidance of a mentor, you will:

Master method development and validation principles (LOD/LOQ, accuracy, precision, matrix effects).
Troubleshoot analytical instrumentation and optimizing extraction efficiency for complex food and water matrices.
Interprete chromatographic and mass-spectral data, including chemometric approaches for quantifying off-flavor compounds.
Understand biological and environmental drivers of off-flavor formation in aquaculture systems.

Description

Crane Conservation Fellowship


Are you passionate about wildlife conservation and eager to contribute to cutting-edge research on endangered species? The International Crane Foundation (ICF) is seeking motivated and passionate individuals for our Crane Conservation Fellowship. This unique opportunity offers hands-on experience working with North America's iconic crane species - Greater Sandhill Cranes and Whooping Cranes - primarily in central Wisconsin. Fellows will be deeply involved in studying crane behavior, ecology, habitat use, and more, contributing directly to conservation efforts that are vital for the long-term survival of these remarkable birds.


The position is located at our Headquarters in Baraboo, WI and runs from March 1, 2027, through February 26, 2028, and includes a stipend of $1,550/month plus housing. Would you like to be surrounded by people who are passionate about our mission, dedicated to the organization, and engaged with their fellow staff and associates? Then read on.


About the Role


As a Crane Conservation Fellow with the International Crane Foundation, you will play an essential role in a variety of research, fieldwork, and outreach efforts supporting crane conservation across the upper Midwest, primarily in Wisconsin. In the field, you will assist in observing color-banded Whooping and Sandhill Cranes to gather data on productivity, habitat use, and breeding pair dynamics. Additional fieldwork will include monitoring avian predator abundance, deploying trail cameras to assess breeding success, measuring nest habitat characteristics, and collecting video behavioral data. The role will also support the capture and banding of both adult and juvenile cranes, collecting environmental samples to aid in the monitoring and conservation of these species.


In addition to fieldwork, you will engage in outreach efforts, sharing the importance of crane conservation with a variety of audiences. This includes engaging with conservation partners and individuals (hunters, landowners, etc.) to promote awareness and protection of cranes in the area. You will have the opportunity to collaborate with ICF staff to design, conduct, and present an independent research project that contributes to the broader scientific understanding of crane populations and their conservation needs. Fellows will gain hands-on experience in ecological restoration, including techniques such as prescribed fire, seed collection, and invasive species control, contributing to the restoration of critical crane habitats.


Qualifications:

Education and Licenses: A Bachelor's degree in Biology or a related field. Graduate students, or those interested in pursuing a graduate degree, are encouraged to apply. A valid driver's license is also required.
Communication Skills: Excellent oral and written communication abilities, including the capacity to convey complex conservation messages to a wide range of audiences, from one-on-one interactions to large presentations.
Attention to Detail: Precision and accuracy are key in ensuring the success of data collection and project implementation.
Interpersonal Skills: Strong ability to build relationships and work collaboratively with diverse groups, including the public, partners, stakeholders, and colleagues across departments.
Physical Stamina: The ability to work long days in the field is a must. Candidates should be comfortable working outdoors in all seasons and in challenging conditions.
Fieldwork & Research Skills: Experience with radio telemetry, behavioral observation, or trail camera deployment is preferred.
Additional Experience: Proficiency in Microsoft Office and experience with environmental education or outreach is preferred.

How to Apply: View the full position description and apply at Job Listings - International Crane Foundation Jobs. The deadline to apply is December 11, 2026.



For more information, or to apply now, you must go to the website below. Please DO NOT email your resume to us as we only accept applications through our website.

OPEN POSITION: Fully Funded M.S. Assistantship – Texas Wildlife Census

Salary: $22,200 annually + tuition, fees, and university benefits

Anticipated Start Date: Spring 2027

Offered by: Texas A&M University, Department of Rangeland, Wildlife and Fisheries Management, in collaboration with the Texas A&M Natural Resources Institute

Research Fields: Wildlife ecology, spatial ecology, camera trapping, quantitative ecology, and biodiversity monitoring

DESCRIPTION

Texas A&M University is seeking applications for a fully funded Master of Science student to work with Drs. Benjamin Hoose and Ty Werdel on the Texas Wildlife Census (TWC), a large-scale wildlife monitoring initiative designed to improve our understanding of wildlife distributions and community composition across Texas.

The Texas Wildlife Census brings together Texas A&M University, the Texas A&M Natural Resources Institute, and the Texas Master Naturalist Program to establish a standardized, volunteer-supported camera-trap monitoring network. The initial phase involves approximately 1,000 trail cameras across the Texas Hill Country, with plans to expand monitoring into additional regions of the state.

The successful candidate will work with a multidisciplinary research team to manage and analyze large camera-trap datasets, investigate wildlife distributions and community patterns, and evaluate the effectiveness of large-scale wildlife monitoring strategies. Potential research topics include species occupancy, wildlife community responses to environmental and land-use gradients, spatial sampling optimization, and the integration of AI-assisted image processing into ecological monitoring. Specific thesis objectives will be developed collaboratively based on the student's interests and project priorities.

This position offers an opportunity to conduct graduate research within an unusually extensive camera-trap monitoring network, develop quantitative and spatial analytical skills, collaborate with natural resource professionals and citizen scientists, and contribute to peer-reviewed publications and conservation efforts across Texas.

Responsibilities will include managing and analyzing camera-trap data, conducting spatial and statistical analyses of wildlife occurrence and community composition, and evaluating sampling designs to improve monitoring efficiency. The successful candidate will also assist with camera deployment coordination, data quality control, and communication with Texas Master Naturalist volunteers and project collaborators. The student will be expected to develop an independent M.S. thesis, prepare manuscripts for peer-reviewed publication, and present findings at professional conferences.

B.S. in wildlife ecology, biology, natural resources management, ecology, or a closely related field

Excellent written and oral communication skills

Valid U.S. driver's license

Experience conducting camera-trap surveys or other wildlife field research

Familiarity with occupancy modeling, spatial statistics, or wildlife community analyses

Experience managing and analyzing large ecological datasets

Experience working with volunteers, private landowners, or conservation partners

Strong technical writing skills and interest in publishing scientific research

Description
Dr. Walter McDonald in the Department of Civil, Construction, and Environmental Engineering at Marquette University is seeking PhD and/or Masters students for two fully-funded graduate research assistantship positions.

Position 1: Remote Sensing of Wetlands and Nature-Based Solutions. The goal of this project is to develop scalable methods for monitoring the condition of restored wetlands, floodplains, and other nature-based solutions using satellite and drone remote sensing. The student will integrate high-resolution imagery, machine learning, and field observations to assess vegetation health, surface water dynamics, and other indicators of restoration condition and maintenance needs. Research will include developing and validating remote sensing methods, evaluating their applicability across sites and seasons, and supporting long-term restoration monitoring. Preference will be given to candidates with backgrounds in environmental or civil engineering, hydrology, remote sensing, GIS, environmental science, machine learning, or related fields.

Position 2: AI-Based Inspection of Stormwater Infrastructure. The goal of this project is to develop automated methods for assessing the condition and maintenance needs of stormwater infrastructure, with an emphasis on stormwater detention ponds. The student will use artificial intelligence, computer vision, and drone and satellite imagery to identify potential maintenance issues, including vegetation overgrowth, sediment accumulation, erosion, and changes in water extent. Research will focus on developing and validating automated inspection tools that can assess infrastructure condition, prioritize maintenance needs, and support large-scale stormwater asset management. Preference will be given to candidates with backgrounds in civil or environmental engineering, computer science, machine learning, computer vision, remote sensing, GIS, or related fields.

The positions have an anticipated start date of Summer or of Fall 2027. Interested candidates should send a statement of interest and a resume to Dr. Walter McDonald ([email removed]), as well as complete a graduate school application at http://www.marquette.edu/grad/future-apply.php/.

Description
The Giery Lab (www.seantgiery.com) in collaboration with the Barrile Lab (gabrielbarrile.weebly.com) in the Department of Zoology & Physiology at the University of Wyoming, is recruiting a graduate student (M.S. preferred; exceptional Ph.D. applicants considered) starting in Fall 2027. 

The student will lead a fully funded project assessing population status and evaluating passive monitoring methods for two high-elevation amphibians of conservation concern in Wyoming: Boreal Toad (Anaxyrus boreas) and Wood Frog (Lithobates sylvaticus). This research is a collaborative project between the University of Wyoming and the Wyoming Game & Fish Department and will provide direct experience translating ecological research into wildlife management and conservation action. In addition to the project’s primary objectives, the student is expected to pursue independent research questions, lead a collaborative field crew, interact directly with state wildlife biologists and land managers, present at regional and national conferences, and lead peer-reviewed manuscripts. 

Location & Fieldwork: The student will be based in Laramie, WY, during the academic year. Fieldwork will occur primarily in remote, high-elevation montane habitats in the Medicine Bow and Bridger-Teton National Forests. Field housing (March–July for at least two field seasons) near Pinedale, WY will be provided with funding available to hire a seasonal field technician. 

Support & Compensation: The position is fully funded for 3 years via a Graduate Research Assistantship that covers a full tuition waiver, mandatory fees, student health insurance, and an annual stipend of approximately $20,856 (M.S.). 

The successful applicant will possess:
A B.S. in wildlife biology, ecology, zoology, natural resources, or a closely related field,
Prior experience assisting with ecological or wildlife field research,
Ability to backpack 10+ miles in rugged terrain, camp remotely, and work under variable weather conditions,
Strong written, oral, and quantitative communication skills,
A valid U.S. driver’s license and eligibility to work in the United States, and
Ability to work effectively both independently and as part of a collaborative team.

Desirable qualifications include:
Amphibian identification, handling, and survey experience,
Familiarity with bioacoustics, database management, and ecological data analysis in R,
Experience coordinating or supervising field crews and off-road driving (4WD),
Experience interacting with state/federal wildlife agencies or non-profit conservation partners, and
A record of technical writing (scientific reports or peer-reviewed manuscripts).

About the Labs: The Giery Lab investigates the evolutionary ecology of wild vertebrates, with an emphasis on reptile and amphibian biology, food webs, infectious disease, and biodiversity in both terrestrial and aquatic systems. The Barrile Lab works at the intersection of disease ecology, population demography, and animal behavior, using techniques in data science and machine learning to inform wildlife management and species conservation.

About the Department & Community: The Department of Zoology & Physiology at UW boasts strong faculty and graduate research groups in vertebrate ecology, evolution, physiology, and disease ecology. Additional information about the UW Dept. of Zoology & Physiology graduate program can be found here: Graduate program information. Laramie (AKA Laradise) is an affordable and laid-back mountain town situated between the Snowy and Laramie Ranges and offers world-class outdoor recreation (hiking, skiing, climbing) and proximity to public lands.

Reach out at [email removed] and [email removed] with questions.

WildCare Oklahoma is a nationally recognized nonprofit organization that provides wildlife and conservation education, technical assistance in resolving human animal conflicts, medical and rehabilitative care to ill, injured, and orphaned wildlife, and members of the public a place to bring native wildlife struggling to survive with the goal of releasing healthy individuals back to nature. WildCare is seeking wildlife rehabilitation & medical fellows to learn about and provide daily rehabilitative care to injured, ill, or orphaned wildlife. This is a paid, full-time fellowship with an established, high-volume wildlife rehabilitation center. You will receive training on animal care protocols and hands-on experience, guided by the professional staff, in WildCare’s wildlife clinic and in the rehabilitative care of mammals, birds, amphibians, and reptiles.

Duties and Responsibilities:

Learn and implement patient protocols by species.
Provide all daily rehabilitative care for wildlife patients in assigned care areas, including feeding and cleaning, treatment, and monitoring patients’ progress.
Learn and implement room/department/nursery cleaning and disinfecting protocols and complete tasks proactively on daily center closing list.
Observe animals’ condition and behavior and report to Rehabilitation Staff, Team Leaders, Rehabilitation Managers, or the veterinary team.
Provide direct support to the veterinary team in the wildlife hospital while learning about the basics of wildlife medicine. Assist with physical therapy and other medical procedures.
Assist veterinary team with animal admissions, intake examinations, and patient record entries.
Carry out maintenance projects at the facility and other projects assigned by Rehabilitation Staff, Team Leaders, or the Rehabilitation Managers.
Take pictures and videos for social media posts; send these to via Group Me app or to a designated email. As time permits, write social media posts and memes, or produce video for submission to marketing personnel (executive director) for use in social media channels.( All pictures or videos taken of WildCare patients while on property or during rescues/releases are the property of WildCare Oklahoma. WildCare gives permission to the individual taking said photos/videos to use these photos in future work with joint attribution to WildCare Oklahoma.)
Carry out assigned releases.
Participate in fellow meetings, rounds, training, and staff meetings.
Complete a self-directed small capstone project designed to showcase your comprehensive learnings from the program.
Participate in four progress check-ins during the fellowship to ensure adequate training and experience is occurring, provide and receive feedback from the Wildlife Rehabilitation Managers, Team Leaders, and other staff, and identify corrective actions on the part of WildCare or the fellow to ensure the best possible experience for the wildlife patients and the highest quality of work from the fellow.

As a fellow, you will have the opportunity to rotate through different departments of the facility based on need, previous experience, personal interest, and progress.

Must be willing to communicate proactively and productively and avoid communication detrimental to team morale or workplace productivity with all team members including WildCare’s dedicated volunteer corps.
Must be willing to follow protocols and instructions to keep self, fellow staff and volunteers, and animals safe.
Must be willing to learn and grow.
Must be comfortable working around humane animal euthanasia
Bachelor’s Degree or coursework  in Biology, Life Sciences, or related field preferred. 
Must have tetanus vaccinations.
Rabies pre-vaccination strongly preferred; a $20/week increase in stipend will be provided with proof of this vaccination.
Wildlife rehabilitation or other animal care experience is strongly preferred. 
Reliable personal vehicle and valid driver’s license required.

Attendance and Dependability - Consistently at work and on time. Follows instructions and responds to management direction. Provides consistent, timely, high-quality work. Follows through on commitments. Uses time efficiently. Takes responsibility for own actions. 
Customer Service - Treats customers (internal and external) with respect and courtesy. Shows interest in, anticipates, and responds timely to customer needs and concerns. Responds appropriately to and resolves difficult and emotional situations. Seeks ways to improve service delivery. 
Diversity - Enthusiastically works with all employees, regardless of race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, culture, and age. Values contributions of people from diverse backgrounds. Demonstrates respect for opinions and ideas of others. Shows awareness of and sensitivity to cultural and individual values. 
Ethics - Tells truth and is honest in all dealings. Avoids situations and actions considered inappropriate or which present a conflict of interest. Upholds organizational values. Does not misrepresent self or use position or authority for personal gain. 
Teamwork - Listens and responds constructively to others' views. Gives and welcomes feedback. Helps others when they need it. Shares expertise. Acknowledges others' effort and contribution. Puts success of the team above own interests. Creates a positive work environment.

The majority of WildCare’s facilities are outdoors. Therefore, candidates for this job must be able to:
Work indoors and outdoors in a wide range of environmental conditions.
Participate in team lifting of animals, weighing up to 300 pounds. Must be able to lift 50 pounds on their own. 
Safely restrain potentially dangerous animals.
Walk, stand, kneel, and crouch indoors and outdoors on uneven terrain in a wide range of weather conditions.
Physically exert themselves at times.
Use all senses every day to evaluate patients—vision, hearing, and hand-eye coordination will be essential for examining and working with wildlife species.

Use a computer to admit patients, update patient records, conduct research to help members of the public, and communicate with WildCare’s constituency.

Fellows should be detail-oriented, should be able to recognize their limitations, and know when to ask for help from staff. Position Title: Ph.D. Graduate Assistantship – Optimizing Invasive Cattail Treatment Effectiveness for Native Vegetation, Waterfowl, and Marsh Birds in Prairie Wetlands

Location: Grand Forks, ND, with field work in western MN (Otter Tail, Pope, Stevens, Traverse, Big Stone, Swift, Chippewa, and Todd counties)

Start Date: Spring 2027 for fieldwork with the potential of a January or August 2027 official grad program start

Position Description: We are seeking a PhD student with broad interest in wetland habitat management and wetland biology/ecology (especially wetland plant, waterfowl, and marsh bird communities) to join a research team comparing the effectiveness and longevity of several treatments for invasive cattail in seasonal prairie pothole wetlands, with the goal of informing habitat management techniques for waterfowl and marsh birds. 

Invasive cattail species (Typha angustifolia, T. x glauca) have dramatically proliferated across North America’s prairie pothole region since the mid-twentieth century. Unlike native cattail, invasive cattail forms thick monocultures, impacting native plant diversity, displacing wildlife food plants, and disrupting habitat structure. The overarching research project is a before-after/control-impact study comparing the outcomes of four cattail treatment methods across approximately 50 wetlands in western Minnesota for the first 3 years following treatment. The selected candidate will collect and analyze post-treatment data, including (1) vegetation type and structure data from vegetation surveys and high-resolution aerial imagery from an uncrewed aerial system (UAS; i.e., a drone), (2) waterfowl and secretive marsh bird abundance from UAS surveys, and (3) waterfowl and secretive marsh bird occupancy from passive acoustic recording units. The selected candidate will analyze these data streams toward the goal of producing practical information for land managers to balance frequency of needed retreatment versus cost per treatment. The candidate will also participate in sharing results with natural resource managers and the public. Given the vast amount of data collected, there is the potential to develop additional questions of interest to the candidate.     

This research is highly collaborative, offering opportunity to engage with professionals in various career tracks and agencies/entities. Partners include scientists and wetland managers from the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources, the US Fish and Wildlife Service, Delta Waterfowl, and the University of Minnesota. Good communication skills will be key to success in this collaborative team.  

This research will have a heavy field travel component, with the PhD student stationed full-time in the field from April to August in 2027, 2028, and possibly 2029. During this time, the student will lead field technicians in data collection. Co-PIs will provide close support, including regular in-person presence. Field work will include piloting UAS’s, driving 4WD trucks and UTVs, hiking across prairie, and wading/collecting data in shallow wetlands with thick emergent vegetation, in a variety of weather conditions (cold early spring to hot summer temperatures).  

Minimum qualifications
·        Master’s degree in plant ecology, wildlife biology, biology, ecology, or a related field
·        Commitment to fostering an inclusive and respectful work environment
·        Strong communication and collaboration skills for working within a large research team
·        Interest in research spanning all project lines of inquiry (wetland management techniques, wetland plant biology/ecology, avian biology/ecology, wetland soils), and research experience pertinent to 1-2 of those topics
·        Willingness to work full-time in the field April-August (with field lodging provided by University of North Dakota)
·        Field work experience relevant to at least one of the project data collection methods
·        Already possess or willing to obtain (with guidance from PIs) a FAA Part 107 license (Remote Pilot Certificate) for operating UAS
·        Experience with statistical analysis of biological data and analysis software (e.g., R)
·        Experience with GIS software (e.g., ArcGIS) 
·        Strong writing skills
·        Experience prioritizing research project tasks and setting realistic timelines for completion

Preferred qualifications
·        Experience leading field crews in data collection
·        At least one peer-reviewed scientific publication
·        Research experience in multiple lines of project inquiry (wetland management techniques, wetland plant biology/ecology, avian biology/ecology, wetland soils) 
·        Field work experience with multiple project data collection methods (e.g., waterfowl surveys using UAS with thermal and EO sensors, plant surveys, passive acoustic recording units, creating orthomosaics from UAS imagery, wetland soil sampling) 

Salary and benefits: $30,240/year plus a tuition waiver. Student is expected to cover the modest student fees that are not an expense that can be covered by grants. The position is primarily funded through a research assistantship through June 2030. The selected candidate will be expected to work a teaching assistantship for 1-2 semesters to develop teaching/mentoring experience and to meet project budget constraints.

Job Description
The Department of Life Sciences at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi (TAMU-CC) invites applications for a 9-month, tenure-track position at the rank of Assistant Professor of Marine Biology. The incumbent will be expected to develop a vigorous, externally funded research program, supervise graduate and undergraduate students, teach undergraduate and graduate courses, contribute to departmental and university services, and pursue scholarly research in support of the department's graduate programs. We particularly welcome applicants with expertise in applied research through collaborations with industry, agencies, community organizations, or other external partners to address challenges and opportunities in coastal management, resilience, health, and sustainability. Experience in workforce readiness education is highly desirable. The appointment is expected to begin in Fall 2027. The position includes a competitive startup package and research lab space.

About the University and Department
Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi is a vibrant, Hispanic and Minority Serving R2 Doctoral Research Institution that proudly provides a solid academic reputation, renowned faculty, and highly rated degree programs since 1947. The University has a heritage of teaching excellence with innovation in research and community engagement as part of the distinguished Texas A&M System. TAMU-CC is the only university in the nation located on its own island, at the heart of the Texas Gulf Coast.

Ample opportunities exist for collaboration within the Department of Life Sciences, departments and research centers within the College of Science and across the campus, and with agencies such as Texas A&M AgriLife. Our unique location and proximity to beaches, wetlands, coastal bays, lagoons, ports, aquaculture operations, and coastal industries provide exceptional opportunities for research, workforce development, and partnerships with the private sector, governmental agencies, and nonprofit organizations.

TAMU-CC has surpassed $50 million in annual research expenditures, reflecting the university’s rapidly growing research enterprise. The university already meets the research expenditure threshold for eligibility in the Texas University Fund (TUF) and is strategically increasing the production of research doctorates. The Department of Life Sciences has 18 full-time tenured or tenure-track faculty, six professional track faculty, two instructors, and over 1,200 science majors (including undergraduate and graduate students) offering B.S. degrees in Biology and Biomedical Science, M.S. degrees in Biology, Marine Biology, and Fisheries and Mariculture, and a Ph.D. degree in Marine Biology. The University of Rhode Island’s Exotic Animal Behavior Lab and Wildlife Genetics and
Ecology Lab are seeking a highly motivated graduate student (PhD) to join our team in Fall 2027
to study the behavior and management of the imperiled New England cottontail rabbit in a
conservation breeding and translocation program. The successful candidate should be interested
in animal personality, genetic mechanisms of breeding behavior, and the role of zoos and state
and federal managers in wildlife conservation.

The research will combine a mix of experimental, field-based, and zoo-based approaches to
advance the conservation of the New England cottontail, a highly collaborative effort with
federal, state, non-profit, and academic partners. The student will be responsible for
investigating: 1) genetic correlates of mate choice decisions in a zoo breeding program; 2) how
animal personality, behavior, rearing environment, and predator detection at release sites interact
to influence survival, and 3) how animal personality influences the behavior of animals after
release. Using these data, the student will be instrumental in developing an evidence-based
translocation strategy to advance the management of this species throughout the Northeastern
US.

Additional responsibilities will include: animal husbandry and care, providing mentorship to
undergraduate students in our vibrant lab setting, field work with state and federal partners to
support trapping and monitoring efforts, analyses of camera trap data to evaluate mammalian
predator detection rates at release sites, supporting ongoing behavior research to inform the
management of the zoo’s breeding program, and using minimally-invasive endocrine methods to
diagnose pregnancy.

The ideal candidate will have excellent written and verbal communication skills, demonstrated
problem-solving skills, a basic statistical background, and an ability to work both independently
and as a productive member of a research team. Applicants should possess a B.S. or B.A.
degree, ideally in biology, wildlife management, animal science, or a related discipline. Preferred
qualifications include a M.S. in a relevant discipline or two years of experience conductingrelated research, experience conducting standard molecular genetic laboratory procedures, experience with behavioral, tagging and/or camera trap data analyses, the development of
machine learning models to measure animal behavior, and field research experience. This
research is primarily conducted on the Kingston, RI campus and field sites in RI on federal and
state properties. We collaborate with partners throughout New England, and therefore the student
may be expected to travel to zoos and field sites as needed in the Northeastern US.

The successful candidate will receive up to 5 years of graduate assistantships consisting
of academic year and summer funding plus a tuition waiver, under the mentorship of Drs. Justin
Richard and T.J. McGreevy, Jr. Interested candidates should send a CV and letter of interest
to Dr. Richard at [email removed]. In addition, interested candidates must have a valid driver’s
license and must be accepted into URI’s College of the Environment and Life Sciences
Biological and Environmental Science graduate program, in the Ecology and Ecosystem Science
specialization (application details at https://web.uri.edu/cels/academics/bes/).

Deadline to apply to URI's graduate program is 12/15/26

Drs. Justin Richard ([email removed]) and T.J. McGreevy ([email removed])

Novel dynamic air-liquid interface (ALI) exposure systems provide a more physiologically relevant approach for evaluating inhalation hazards by exposing airway cells directly to airborne chemicals; however, substantial challenges remain in characterizing and standardizing these systems for volatile chemical exposures. ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), Genomics and Bioinformatics Research Unit, located in Gainesville, Florida.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: The H5N1 outbreak in U.S. dairy cattle showed that influenza can establish itself in mammalian hosts and that our surveillance tools must keep pace with a changing virus. This fellowship combines two efforts: making PCR-based diagnostics and sequencing assays robust to viral mutation, and tracking viral adaptation to mammals through structural modeling. You will have the freedom to set the balance between them with your mentor, based on your strengths and early results.

Project 1: Predicting assay failure as the virus mutates. With your mentor, you will learn how to build machine-learning models that predict how primer-template mismatches reduce amplification and extension efficiency in avian influenza assays, so likely failures can be flagged before they affect testing. You will use a large molecular training dataset and validate against new data from federal partner labs at the National Poultry Research Center and National Animal Disease Center. This is one of a set of foundational PCR modeling projects pairing optimization and ML methods for multiplex primer design: our group recently published PRISM (Chen et al., Bioinformatics, 2026), a submodular-optimization framework that designs multiplex primers. A central question is how to bring mismatch-aware predictions into this design framework. This learning experience is a collaboration with Dr. David Suarez, who developed the key avian influenza diagnostic tests.

Project 2: Predicting receptor-binding shifts. With your mentor, you will learn how to develop structure-based approaches to estimate how hemagglutinin and neuraminidase variants interact with avian-type (a2,3) and human-type (a2,6) sialic acid receptors, toward scalable monitoring of mammalian adaptation. This is a new direction for the lab, and we are still identifying potential structural-biology collaborators. Methods may include AlphaFold-based modeling, glycan-aware docking or co-folding, and OpenMM with AMBER-family force fields.

Several past mentees came in from a wet-lab or biology background and left with strong computational skills - training people across that boundary is as much a part of this fellowship as the research itself. Fellows publish as first author, and leave with an open-source tool and a dataset others will use. We support travel to present and collaborate closely with the University of Florida Emerging Pathogens Institute and the Microbiology and Cell Science department. Our workflows are Python-based and moving toward Rust; we provide training either direction, and we use AI-assisted coding with code review.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will:

Learn how viral evolution influences the reliability of PCR-based diagnostics for avian influenza and other rapidly changing pathogens while developing computational primer-design and optimization approaches for multiplex PCR assays.
Develop skills in machine learning, molecular-data analysis, and structural biology by modeling primer–template mismatches, studying influenza protein adaptation to mammalian receptors, and using tools such as AlphaFold-based protein modeling, glycan-aware docking, and molecular-dynamics simulations.
Gain experience validating computational predictions with laboratory-generated diagnostic data from federal animal-health research partners while building an understanding of influenza virology, molecular diagnostics, viral host adaptation, and zoonotic-disease surveillance.
Strengthen programming and research-computing skills in Python, with opportunities to learn Rust, collaborative software development, code review, AI-assisted coding practices, and the development of reproducible open-source research tools and datasets.
Build interdisciplinary research, scientific communication, and professional skills through collaboration across biology, virology, bioinformatics, machine learning, and structural modeling, as well as through conference presentations and first-author publication opportunities.
Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Adam Rivers ([email removed]). Dr. Adam Rivers is a coauthor of QIIME 2, a widely used bioinformatics platform, and developer of tools including ITSxpress, Guidemaker, Branchwater, and Tamipami. The lab builds open, reproducible software that other scientists adopt. If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor.

Get paid to work outdoors, gain hands-on natural resource management experience, and help manage America's public lands!

The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) is hiring seasonal Range Technicians for the 2027 field season at locations throughout the Western United States. These positions offer an excellent opportunity for college students, recent graduates, and individuals interested in rangeland management, natural resources, wildlife biology, ecology, agriculture, botany, and environmental science to gain practical experience working on public lands.

Range Technicians work alongside professional resource specialists and land managers to monitor and manage millions of acres of public rangelands. This is hands-on fieldwork where you will gain experience with vegetation monitoring, grazing management, natural resource inventories, invasive plant management, and rangeland improvement projects.

What You'll Do
Depending on the location and specific position, duties may include:
Conduct vegetation surveys, rangeland inventories, and ecological monitoring.
Collect field data on vegetation, soils, livestock grazing, water resources, and rangeland conditions.
Assist with grazing allotment inspections and monitoring livestock use on public lands.
Identify invasive and noxious weeds and assist with weed management projects.
Assist with the construction, inspection, and maintenance of rangeland improvements, including fences and water developments.
Use GPS, GIS, maps, and other field technology to collect and manage resource information.
Assist with wildlife habitat and other natural resource management projects.

Rangeland Management and Range Science
Natural Resources Management
Wildlife Biology and Wildlife Management
Ecology and Environmental Science
Botany and Plant Science
Agriculture and Animal Science

Forestry and Conservation

Description
Paid Student Internship 
San Francisco Public Utilities Commission (SFPUC) 
Natural Resources and Lands Management Division, Biological Resources Group

Internship Overview 

Are you excited about working outdoors protecting natural resources? Do you love nature, ecology, plants and wildlife? If so, this could be the PAID internship for you! We are looking for a motivated intern to work with the Biological Resources Group to help protect and restore the natural resources of the San Francisco Peninsula on SFPUC lands. Our work includes surveying for rare and endangered plants and animals, identifying and managing threats to sensitive species, supporting vegetation management projects including prescribed burns, controlling invasive species, planting native species, and restoring habitats for rare and endangered animals. Based out of Millbrae, your “office” stretches from the remote valleys of the San Andreas Reservoir near San Bruno to the Upper Crystal Springs Reservoir near Woodside. Work in a variety of habitats from Douglas fir and redwood forests to steep scrublands and rare serpentine grasslands. Help to protect state and federally listed animals such as the Mission blue butterfly, San Francisco garter snake, California red-legged frog, and a variety of threatened, endangered, or rare plant species. Gain experience with environmental specialties such as botany, wildlife biology, vegetation management, hydrology, forestry, integrated pest management, fisheries, environmental laws and regulations, compliance, and planning. Gain a professional network with experienced staff and environmental consultants. 

Description of Duties and Learning Objectives 
The successful candidates will join SFPUC biologists in a variety of natural resource management projects and will learn how to:
• Survey for rare and listed plants and animals and monitor projects to ensure their protection.
• Monitor vegetation communities and planting survivorship.
• Monitor threatened and endangered wildlife such as California red-legged frogs, Mission blue and San Bruno elfin butterflies
• Remove invasive species using hand tools, power tools, herbicide, and other methods.
• Revegetate disturbed landscapes with native plants.
• Map key habitat features using ArcGIS, ESRI Field Maps, Arc GIS Online; analyze and display mapped features using GIS technology.
• Evaluate progress toward mitigation goals; collect, enter, and manage ecological data.
• Prepare reports and correspondence relating to conservation projects.
• Maintain tools and equipment and other miscellaneous duties.

Washington State University (WSU) seeks a visionary leader for the position of Director of the School of the Environment (SOE) in the College of Arts and Sciences (CAS) and the College of Agricultural, Human, and Natural Resource Sciences (CAHNRS).

The Director provides academic and administrative leadership for SOE, a multi-college and multi-campus enterprise from the Pullman campus. The School Director position is a 12-month academic termed position, through renewable, administrative leadership appointment, as well as either a permanent full-time 9-month tenure-eligible position at the rank of Professor (a successful Professor candidate will have an expedited tenure review upon acceptance of the position), or as a continuous full-time 9-month Career-Track position at the rank of Professor. The Center for Conservation Technology & Innovation (CTI) at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute (NZCBI) seeks an intern to investigate the environmental factors driving the development of vegetation patches at latrines created by vicuña (Vicugna vicugna). One of four camelid species native to the tropical highlands of South America, vicuña represent a conservation success story: after decades of extensive harvesting and hunting, regulation and conservation actions led to their recovery. Now, emerging evidence indicates that vicuña-initiated vegetation patches accelerate ecological succession in glacial forefields by more than 150 years. However, the conditions under which patches develop from latrines, and the distances over which patches exert ecological influence, are not well-understood. This internship will compile multiple types of field data, and compile and derive remote sensing variables (e.g., topographical variables, proximity to water, and proximity to climax vegetation communities) for vegetation patches and control sites in the Cordillera Vilcanota, Peru. The selected intern will analyze high-resolution remote sensing data to assess vegetation productivity around vicuña-initiated patches, and use a variance partitioning approach to evaluate which factors influence patch establishment and characteristics (e.g., area, vegetation cover, microbial abundance and diversity, and primary production).

Responsibilities:
-        Manage libraries of remote sensing imagery, GIS products, field data, and scripts in multiple programming languages 
-        Use Python, R, Google Earth Engine, and/or GIS software (e.g., QGIS, ArcGIS) to derive novel covariates from field and remote sensing data 
-        Visualize complex, spatially explicit data sets and analysis results
-        Integrate field, remote sensing, hydrological, topographical, and geomorphological data into efficient analysis workflows
-        Implement variance partitioning models that include multiple predictor and response variables
-        Work with mentor and collaborators to develop a scientific manuscript describing the ecological factors driving establishment and growth, and the approximate area of influence, of vicuña-initiated vegetation patches in the tropical Andes
 The ideal candidate will...

-        Possess at least an undergraduate degree in ecology, GIS or remote sensing, wildlife biology, environmental sciences, or a similar field (master’s degree preferred but not required).
-        Have previous experience with complex workflows in GIS, remote sensing, or another spatially explicit analysis context.
-        Have experience in python or R, Google Earth Engine, and/or QGIS or ArcGIS.
-        Have strong attention to detail, professionalism, and organizational skills; and work well both independently and in a small team.
-        Be available for at least 6 months beginning in December 2026 / January 2027.
 This six-month internship will begin in December 2026 or January 2027, with the possibility for extension. Salary will be $400-650/week depending on experience and qualifications, with housing provided at the SCBI campus in Front Royal, VA. The intern will work closely with researchers in CTI and James Madison University (JMU), with occasional local travel to Harrisonburg, VA. When possible, the intern will be encouraged to participate in other research projects and fieldwork opportunities. All NZCBI interns have access to regular seminars and skills workshops related to applied conservation, field ecology, quantitative ecology, animal movement, animal behavior, GIS, and remote sensing. 
 To apply, please send 1) a cover letter describing your interest, qualifications, relevant experience, and long-term career goals; 2) a current resume or CV; and 3) contact information for 2-3 references to [email removed]. Please include your earliest possible start date and the total time for which you are available. 
 SCBI is located in Front Royal, VA, about 70 miles west of Washington, DC near the north entrance of Shenandoah National Park. SCBI plays a leading role in the Smithsonian’s efforts to save wildlife species from extinction and train future generations of conservationists.

One of four camelid species native to the tropical highlands of South America, vicuña represent a conservation success story: after decades of extensive harvesting and hunting, regulation and conservation actions led to their recovery. Now, emerging evidence indicates that vicuña-initiated vegetation patches accelerate ecological succession in glacial forefields by more than 150 years. However, the conditions under which patches develop from latrines, and the distances over which patches exert ecological influence, are not well-understood. This internship will compile multiple types of field data, and compile and derive remote sensing variables (e.g., topographical variables, proximity to water, and proximity to climax vegetation communities) for vegetation patches and control sites in the Cordillera Vilcanota, Peru. The selected intern will analyze high-resolution remote sensing data to assess vegetation productivity around vicuña-initiated patches, and use a variance partitioning approach to evaluate which factors influence patch establishment and characteristics (e.g., area, vegetation cover, microbial abundance and diversity, and primary production).

Responsibilities:
-        Manage libraries of remote sensing imagery, GIS products, field data, and scripts in multiple programming languages 
-        Use Python, R, Google Earth Engine, and/or GIS software (e.g., QGIS, ArcGIS) to derive novel covariates from field and remote sensing data 
-        Visualize complex, spatially explicit data sets and analysis results
-        Integrate field, remote sensing, hydrological, topographical, and geomorphological data into efficient analysis workflows
-        Implement variance partitioning models that include multiple predictor and response variables
-        Work with mentor and collaborators to develop a scientific manuscript describing the ecological factors driving establishment and growth, and the approximate area of influence, of vicuña-initiated vegetation patches in the tropical Andes
 The ideal candidate will...

-        Possess at least an undergraduate degree in ecology, GIS or remote sensing, wildlife biology, environmental sciences, or a similar field (master’s degree preferred but not required).
-        Have previous experience with complex workflows in GIS, remote sensing, or another spatially explicit analysis context.
-        Have experience in python or R, Google Earth Engine, and/or QGIS or ArcGIS.
-        Have strong attention to detail, professionalism, and organizational skills; and work well both independently and in a small team.
-        Be available for at least 6 months beginning in December 2026 / January 2027.
 This six-month internship will begin in December 2026 or January 2027, with the possibility for extension. Salary will be $400-650/week depending on experience and qualifications, with housing provided at the SCBI campus in Front Royal, VA. The intern will work closely with researchers in CTI and James Madison University (JMU), with occasional local travel to Harrisonburg, VA. When possible, the intern will be encouraged to participate in other research projects and fieldwork opportunities. All NZCBI interns have access to regular seminars and skills workshops related to applied conservation, field ecology, quantitative ecology, animal movement, animal behavior, GIS, and remote sensing. 
 To apply, please send 1) a cover letter describing your interest, qualifications, relevant experience, and long-term career goals; 2) a current resume or CV; and 3) contact information for 2-3 references to [email removed]. Please include your earliest possible start date and the total time for which you are available. 
 SCBI is located in Front Royal, VA, about 70 miles west of Washington, DC near the north entrance of Shenandoah National Park. SCBI plays a leading role in the Smithsonian’s efforts to save wildlife species from extinction and train future generations of conservationists.

Position Title: Land and Water Conservation Fund Records and Program Support Fellow – AmeriCorps

Conservation Legacy Program: Stewards Individual Placements

Site Location: 601 Riverfront Drive Omaha, NE 68102

 

Terms of Service:

· End Date: 01/31/2028

· AmeriCorps Slot Classification: 1700 Hours

 

Purpose:

Stewards Individual Placements (Stewards), a program of Conservation Legacy, provides individuals with AmeriCorps service and career opportunities to strengthen communities and preserve our natural resources. Participants serve with federal agencies, tribal governments, and nonprofits to provide institutional capacity, develop community relationships, and support ecosystem health. Stewards in partnership with the NPS Land and Water Conservation Fund will host a Records and Program Support Fellow.

The NPS Land and Water Conservation Fund Stateside Assistance Program supports outdoor recreation through grants to states and local governments across all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories. Properties funded through this grant program are required to be encumbered for outdoor recreation use in perpetuity which necessitates various ongoing stewardship requirements. This AmeriCorps position will support the overall administration of the LWCF Stateside Assistance program through improving access and discoverability of records pertaining to these properties and the original grants which encumbered them. Additionally, they will be tasked with creating, updating, and improving internal and external program resources and assisting program staff with grant administration. While the member will primarily serve directly with program staff day-to-day in resolving records management issues, developing internal and external program resources, and supporting grant management

processes, their service ultimately will have a broader impact on the program’s ability to serve our grantees better and promote outdoor recreation nationally.

 

Description of Duties:

The member(s) will serve closely with the Records and Information Management Specialist to perform a variety of records management functions including:

· Appraisal and arrangement of federal records, including assisting with transfers of records to Federal Records Centers and/or the National Archives

· Completing inventories for program records to establish intellectual control

· Assisting staff with requests for historical program records

The member(s) will serve closely with an Outdoor Recreation Planner (Program Officer) to perform a variety of administrative functions including:

· Organize and maintain internal program files, records, and SharePoint resources to improve staff access to information

· Develop, update, and enhance internal SharePoint pages and workflows to increase efficiency and improve staff experience

· Administer user membership for external SharePoint site, coordinating permissions and access requests with internal and external partners

· Coordinate quarterly content reviews and updates of external SharePoint resources to ensure information remains accurate, current, and able to be accessed

· Assist program staff with grant management activities, including application intake, tribal consultation, grant review coordination, records organization, and administrative support throughout the grant lifecycle

 

Qualifications:

· United States citizen, United States national, or a lawful permanent resident alien

· At least 17 years of age

· Has received a high school diploma or equivalency certificate; or has not dropped out of elementary or secondary school to enroll as an AmeriCorps participant, and agrees to obtain a high school diploma or its equivalent prior to using the education award

· Agrees to provide information to establish eligibility and to complete a National Service Criminal History Check.

· Has received a Bachelor’s degree.

· Ability to lift minimum of 40 lbs (weight of a standard records box).

· Ability to work independently on projects.

· Preference for candidates with previous clerical/administrative, records management, information management, library science, and/or archival experience.

· Preference for candidates with interest in outdoor recreation and/or federal grants management.

· Preference for candidates with a Master’s degree in a related field.

 

Our Commitment:

Conservation Legacy is committed to the full consideration of all qualified individuals and will ensure that persons with disabilities are provided reasonable accommodations to perform essential job functions. Physical requirements may include periodic overnight travel, non-traditional work hours, ability to move across varied terrain, use program-specific tools and a range of technology on an infrequent or frequent basis. Exerting up to 25 pounds of force occasionally to lift, carry, push, pull, or otherwise move objects. The ability to safely drive an organizational vehicle may also be required for some positions. If you need assistance and/or reasonable accommodation due to a disability during the application or recruiting process, please send a request to Vanessa Morrison at [email removed]

 

Time Requirements:

· Typically, this position is expected to serve 9 am to 5 pm, but exact service schedules may vary. A half hour lunch break will not be counted towards AmeriCorps service.

· Member may be required to participate in national, state, or local service projects or events as part of their service term.

Orientation and Training:

· Member will receive an orientation that includes training on AmeriCorps prohibited and unallowable activities.

· Member will complete additional NPS-required trainings for system access.

· Member will receive additional on-the-job training for specific records management and administrative tasks, as needed.

 

Benefits:

· Segal AmeriCorps Education Award of $7,395.00

· Living Allowance of $600.00 per week.

· Additional Benefit of $400.00 per week.

· Healthcare Coverage if Eligible

· Childcare Coverage if Eligible

· Loan forbearance if Eligible

· Interest Payments if Eligible

 

Evaluation and Reporting:

As an AmeriCorps member, performance will be evaluated on whether the member has completed the required number of hours, the member has satisfactorily completed assignments, and if the member has met other performance criteria that were clearly communicated at the beginning of the term of service.

Reporting requirements include, but are not limited to, bi-weekly timesheets and accomplishment tracking.

Stewards Contact Information: Emma Nehan-Springstead, [email removed]

NPS Contact information: · Joy Pierce, [email removed] · Matt Colwin, [email removed]

 

 

Conservation Legacy is an equal opportunity employer, and all qualified applicants will receive consideration for employment without regard to race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, pregnancy, age, national origin, disability status, genetic information, protected veteran status, or any other characteristic protected by law.

We also consider qualified applicants regardless of criminal histories, consistent with legal requirements. If you need assistance and/or reasonable accommodations due to a disability during the application or recruiting process, please send a request to the hiring manager.

Description

Summary
American Conservation Experience, a nonprofit Conservation Corps, in partnership with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS), is seeking 1 member to contribute to wetland easement mapping, data management, and communication projects under the mentorship of U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Staff.

For more information about ACE, please visit our website.

Start Date: January 2027 (Flexible)

Estimated End Date: October 2027 (Flexible)

*a 40 week minimum commitment is required, approximately 1600 hours*

Location Details/Description: Eastern South Dakota National Wildlife Refuge Complex- Waubay National Wildlife Refuge (NWR), Waubay, SD

The Wetland Management Districts were established to help restore and preserve the vital habitats of the Prairie Pothole Region of North America. This region is filled with wetlands, lakes, and rolling hills. It was formed by glaciers as they melted and moved through the area more than 10,000 years ago. Today, nearly half of all ducks that hatch in the continental United States come from the Prairie Pothole Region.

For more information, please visit the FWS website. 

Position Overview: The mission of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) is working with others to conserve, protect, and enhance fish, wildlife, plants, and their habitats for the continuing benefit of the American people. This position will help FWS realize that mission. 

Duties will primarily involve supporting wetland easement mapping negotiations, including collecting and verifying landowner and easement information, identifying and mapping wetlands, and a variety of other communication and data management tasks. Specific duties include:
Collecting data from landowner requests related to wetland easements. 
Identifying temporary and ephemeral wetlands using various tools (National Wetland Index, Georeferenced historical satellite images, ground truthing, etc.).
Scanning easement documents and providing GIS data/layers.
Producing draft maps using GIS.
Supporting data and records management by building and managing file structures and tracking data.
Drafting responses to landowners for manager review and signature.
Supporting data requests from FWS and track file status for on-going requests.
Developing land acquisition proposals for wetland easements.
Assisting Cartography and Realty teams by editing and attributing datasets, reviewing maps and associated data, managing files, and producing cartographic products.
Assisting with tile setback requests by collecting data, issuing permits, coordinating with staff, and conducting field checks.
Assisting with planning/coordination and ensuring compliance with FWS standards associated with wetland areas identified for restoration.
Providing remote support to other stations throughout the Prairie Pothole Region.
This individual placement is meant to facilitate professional development and promotes exposure to land management agencies and networking with professionals. This could include gaining experience in different conservation fields and shadowing different work groups.

Schedule: Duties will primarily be carried out Monday - Friday. Bi-weekly totals should not exceed 80 hours. A flexible work schedule may be required, which could involve work performed outside of normal work hours including on weekends and/or holidays. Time off may be granted and requests should be directed to ACE and the FWS for approval.

Position Benefits
Living Allowance: The ACE Member is expected to contribute ~40 hours/week and will receive a living allowance of $850/week to offset the costs of food and incidental expenses, dispersed bi-weekly.

Public Land Corps Hiring Authority: Members serving under this agreement may be eligible for a federal hiring authority upon completion of their term of service and 640 hours of service. If the duration of a PLC-eligible term is not long enough for Members to accrue 640 hours of service (~16 weeks), the total hours served at the completion of the term may be eligible to be combined with hours accrued from another PLC-eligible term to meet the 640 hours requirement. PLC projects also include specific eligibility requirements such as age and citizenship. Please contact ACE staff with questions about eligibility, or view general eligibility information on our website.

Housing: ACE members will be accommodated in provided FWS housing at no cost for the duration of the term.

Relocation Allowance: ACE members will have up to $1,100 to be used for eligible relocation expenses to be split at the beginning and end of the term. Eligible relocation expenses for this position include mileage, hotels, meals, etc., and must have a receipt for reimbursement. Additional expenses must be approved by ACE staff prior to purchase. Further details regarding distribution of these funds will be provided during the interview process.

Gear Reimbursement: ACE members will have up to $200 to spend on eligible gear purchases. Eligible gear for this position includes, socks, boots, work pants, outerwear, sunglasses, office supplies/needs, etc., and must be approved by ACE staff prior to purchase. 

Provided Training/Orientation: ACE members will receive position specific training and an orientation outlining ACE policies and procedures, clear guidance on prohibited activities, and networks for support. Specific training may include Defensive Driving, ATV/UTV, Aerial Surveys for Wetland Easement Monitoring.

Qualifications
Required:
Members must be authorized to work in the United States. ACE does not provide sponsorship for employment visas. 
Willing and able to represent ACE and the partner organization in a professional, positive, and enthusiastic manner. 
Ability to be both self-directed/work alone, and be a positive, contributing member of a group.
A valid driver's license and an insurable driving record (documentation to be provided upon request). Members must be 21+ to drive due to ACE's insurance and liability requirements.
Willing to undergo and must pass the required criminal history checks 
Ability to perform the essential duties of the position with or without reasonable accommodation.
ACE Members will need to complete bi-weekly timesheets, beginning of term feedback forms, end of term evaluations and for longer terms, a mid-term evaluation. 
Member may not participate in any prohibited activities as listed in the Member Service Agreement.
To learn more about eligibility requirements, please visit our website. 

Preferred:
Competitive applicants for this position hold a Bachelor's or Master's degree in the natural resources field and/or have relevant experience in subject areas such as natural resource management, GIS, data management, wildlife biology, and/or other related disciplines related to this position.
Knowledge of data management, data entry, and data summarization
Experience using various data management software: Microsoft Excel, AGOL, ArcPro
Deep interest in wildlife conservation and the USFWS mission.

Physical Demands, Work Environment and Working Conditions: 
Physical Demands: Requires frequent sitting, standing, walking, hiking, carrying, using hands to handle or feel, reaching with hands and arms, talking and hearing. Manual dexterity required for use of various tools, computer keyboard/mouse and other office equipment. Required to stoop, kneel, climb stairs, and/or crouch.
Vision Requirements: Requires close, distance, peripheral and depth perception vision as well as the ability to focus. 
Weight Lifted or Force Exerted: Frequently moves up to 10 lbs., ability to move up to 25 pounds.
Environmental: Outdoor and indoor conditions. Work environment conditions can change frequently; working under adverse weather conditions and in various climates.
Noise Environment: Moderate noise such as in a business office with equipment and light traffic.
Travel: This position does not require unique travel.

Environmental Conditions/Hazards: The ACE member(s) may encounter environmental conditions/hazards including extreme heat or cold, rocky terrain, swamp or wetland conditions, biting insects, and potentially dangerous wildlife. The member is expected to conduct duties in a safe and orderly manner so as not to endanger self, fellow staff/members or resources. 

Vehicle and Equipment Use/Safety: If a vehicle is required for the accomplishment of the duties, one will be provided by the FWS or ACE. Any tools required for the accomplishment of the duties will be provided by the FWS. Use of personal protective equipment (PPE), typically provided by the FWS, will be mandatory for any activity that requires it. Strict adherence to FWS and ACE equipment training, certification and safety protocols is required. 

To Apply: Please submit your resume, a cover letter demonstrating your interest and experience, and contact information for three professional/academic references to ACE's online application page for this position on our website.Early consideration will be given as applications are received. This position may close at any time. If you have any questions regarding this position please feel free to contact ACE EPIC FWS Member Manager, Saige Ruleau.

If you meet at least 70 percent of the qualifications, we want to hear from you!

ACE participates in E-Verify and will provide the federal government with your Form I-9 information when you are enrolled in a program to confirm that you are authorized to work in the U.S.

EEO: Employment or Service with ACE is based upon ability, qualifications, attitude, and job-related factors. Every qualified employee, member, or applicant has the same opportunity for recruitment, hire, training, transfer, promotion, compensation, demotion, termination, benefits, employee activities, and general treatment without regard to race, color, religion, age, sex, creed, national origin, pregnancy, ancestry, citizenship status, genetic information, veteran or military status, physical or mental disability, sexual orientation, medical condition, marital or parental status, political affiliation, ethnicity, hair texture or style, arrest record, caste, hereditary status, endogamy, or any other classification protected by applicable local, state, or federal law.

Fisheries Individual Placement – AmeriCorps (2 openings)

  Term of Service:
Start Date: 2/1/2027
End Date: 7/30/2027
AmeriCorps Slot Classification: 900 Hours 
  Purpose:
This is an AmeriCorps position with Arizona Conservation Corps (AZCC), which is an AmeriCorps program of Conservation Legacy. The members selected for this position will be serving at the Safford, AZ BLM office as an AmeriCorps members with Arizona Conservation Corps, and completing service projects for the Bureau of Land Management. 
 AZCC aims to continue the legacy of the Civilian Conservation Corps of the 1930's, and is focused on connecting youth, young adults, and recent era military veterans with communities and conservation service projects on public lands. AZCC operates programs across Arizona that engage individuals and strengthen communities through service and conservation. AZCC has program offices in Flagstaff, Tucson, and Phoenix. 
  Partner Agency:
The BLM Safford Field Office (SFO) manages 1.4 million acres of deserts, mountains and grasslands in six eastern Arizona counties and another 118,000 acres of rangelands in New Mexico in cooperation with the BLM Las Cruces District Office. Its boundaries range from the Navajo Nation in the north to the international boundary with Mexico in the south. There are eight units within BLM’s National Landscape Conservation System, including the Gila Box Riparian National Conservation Area, six wilderness areas, including the world-renowned Aravaipa Canyon Wilderness and one wilderness study area. 
 Public lands in this field office also include 11 Areas of Critical Environmental Concern, Muleshoe Ranch Cooperative Management Area, Black Hills Back Country Byway, Willcox Playa National Natural Landmark, Guadalupe Canyon Outstanding Natural Area, one property on the National Register of Historic Places and more than 30 miles of stream segments under consideration for Wild & Scenic River designation. 
 The Safford Field Office and partners have been working to gather current and accurate information on the distribution and abundance of non-native fish species on BLM managed public lands. The information is then used to target removal efforts in those habitats supporting non-native predatory fish. 
  Description of Duties:
Working under the Fisheries Biologist, the selected Individual Placements or “members” will assist with fish habitat improvement in the Gila Box Riparian National Conservation Area and Aravaipa Ecosystem Management Area, which includes the Aravaipa Canyon Wilderness, and will be helping to secure four federally endangered fish populations and populations of five sensitive fish species that are currently being impacted by non-native fish. Through their involvement, the members will learn about conservation practices and invasive species management. 
 The members will work together to mechanically remove nonnative fishes, specifically Yellow Bullhead (Ameiurus natalis) from Bonita and Aravaipa Creeks, whose presence threatens native fish. The members will work directly with Safford's fisheries biologist and contractors for the first month or so, until they are confident and comfortable with the equipment and with fish identification. At that time, they will frequently work independently in the field.   
 The members will be responsible for data collection in the field, data entry in the office, and data review and quality control. They will have the opportunity to conduct fish monitoring in multiple habitats across the field office and interact with partner agencies and organizations. 
 Additionally, the members will work with the fisheries biologist to improve habitat conditions within five priority wildlife exclosures for native fish species, and resident and migratory wildlife. This work entails bank stabilization, seeding and planting of native vegetation, removal of invasive plant and trees species, and installation of erosion control structures. Bank stabilization along the wetted habitat is necessary to prevent bank sloughing and excess sediment from entering the aquatic habitat. Rock and gravel along with native grasses and forbs will be used to stabilize the banks, which will also function as a riparian buffer to filter nonpoint source pollutants from incoming runoff. The transition zone between riparian and terrestrial habitats will be stabilized with trees and grasses. Rock rundowns will be constructed along the terrestrial habitat to allow non-erosive runoff to enter the aquatic habitat.
 These projects will help strengthen partnerships with federal, state, city, and non-governmental organizations that collaborate on behalf of desert fish conservation. Work with BLM SFO fisheries biologist and contractors to remove nonnative fish from Bonita and Aravaipa Creeks, and enhance and improve habitat conditions within five priority wildlife exclosures.

Work directly with fisheries biologist or contractors on habitat restoration projects. 
Utilize Hydrolab equipment to monitor water quality.
Perform seeding and native vegetation plantings.
