Description

Help Shape the Future of Wisconsin’s Forests

What if your work could help private landowners build healthier forests and better wildlife habitat in Wisconsin? The Ruffed Grouse Society & American Woodcock Society (RGS & AWS) is seeking a Forest Wildlife Specialist to work alongside the Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS), bringing forest management expertise and conservation programs directly to landowners.


Background and Description:


Established in 1961, the Ruffed Grouse Society (RGS) is North America’s foremost conservation organization dedicated to creating healthy forests, abundant wildlife, and promoting a conservation ethic. Together with the American Woodcock Society (AWS), established in 2014, RGS & AWS work with private landowners and government agencies to develop critical wildlife habitat utilizing scientific management practices. RGS & AWS is a national organization with a 65-year record of forest wildlife conservation.


RGS & AWS has entered into a collaborative agreement with the Natural Resources Conservation Services (NRCS). Together, RGS & AWS and NRCS are looking for a motivated individual to work effectively with private landowners and other stakeholders in the southern Driftless region of Wisconsin. The Forest Wildlife Specialist will function as a Wildlife Forester, providing conservation technical assistance to private landowners.


Why This Role Matters

RGS & AWS works with private landowners and public agencies to advance science-based forest management and wildlife conservation. Through a collaborative agreement with NRCS, this position will provide practical technical assistance to private landowners, helping them plan and implement forest management that increases forest diversity and benefits wildlife, especially young forest habitats.

You will serve as a Wildlife Forester, connecting landowners with Farm Bill conservation opportunities, developing forest management plans, and coordinating with NRCS, Wisconsin DNR (WDNR), RGS & AWS, and other partners. This is a hands-on role with substantial time in the field and opportunities to make conservation happen on private lands.


What You’ll Accomplish

Landowner Assistance and Forest Planning

•  Provide one-on-one technical assistance to private landowners and assess forest and wildlife habitat conditions.

•  Develop site-specific forest management plans and recommendations that connect silviculture, forest diversity, and wildlife habitat objectives.

•  Help landowners access and implement the Environmental Quality Incentives Program (EQIP), Conservation Stewardship Program (CSP), and other federal, state, and local conservation programs.

•  Use ArcGIS, Field Maps, and other mapping tools to delineate projects, document conditions, and support management decisions.

Project Implementation and Monitoring

•  Support conservation contract development and coordination, site assessments, implementation, and monitoring of forest management practices.

•  Coordinate with NRCS, WI DNR, RGS & AWS, and other partners to advance young forest restoration and habitat improvement.

•  Track and report accomplishments, project progress, and conservation outcomes.

Outreach and Partner Coordination

•  Develop and deliver outreach and educational activities that encourage adoption of active forest management.

•  Participate in relevant RGS & AWS, NRCS, and WDNR meetings and collaborate with conservation partners.

•  As needed, assist with regional conservation projects on public and private lands and participate in RGS & AWS member or fundraising events.


What We’re Looking For

Must-Haves

•  A degree in forestry or a closely related field, with two or more years of experience and/or a graduate degree in natural resource management.

•  Strong knowledge of forest ecology, forest management, silviculture, forest operations, wildlife habitat, and relevant environmental regulations.

•  Ability to develop site-specific forest management plans and apply active forest management to silvicultural and wildlife objectives.

•  Strong communication, public speaking, organization, and relationship-building skills, including comfort working directly with private landowners.

•  Ability to use Microsoft Word, Excel, ArcGIS, Field Maps, and other mapping systems.

•  Self-direction, problem-solving ability, and experience managing multiple projects and deadlines.

•  A valid driver’s license, willingness to complete required partner training, and ability to travel frequently and perform physically demanding fieldwork in difficult terrain and varied weather.

Experience That Would Set You Apart

•  Professional forestry or wildlife habitat management experience in the Western Great Lakes.

•  Experience working with private landowners and federal or state conservation programs.

•  Familiarity with forest harvesting systems, habitat improvement practices, and translating forest management plans into on-the-ground work.


Work Environment and Benefits

This position is based in Richland Center, Wisconsin, and involves remote work, office-based tasks, and regular travel for fieldwork, meetings, and events across north-central Wisconsin. Fieldwork is expected to account for approximately 75% of the workload. The position includes a six-month probationary period and is a term appointment expected to run through September 2028, with a likely extension.

The starting salary range is $50,000–$59,900, based on qualifications, experience, training, certifications, and organizational needs. Merit increases may be available based on performance. Benefits include paid time off; medical, dental, and vision insurance; retirement options with employer contribution; a vehicle or business mileage reimbursement; a purchasing card for authorized expenses; computer and printer; cell phone; and office supplies.


Join Us

Interested in helping Wisconsin landowners improve forests and wildlife habitat? Email a cover letter and resume combined into a single PDF, along with three references, to [email removed]. Use “WI Forest Wildlife Specialist” as the email subject line. The posting lists December 13, 2026, as the closing date, or until filled with an exceptional candidate. Questions can be directed to Jared Elm at (715) 450-2531 or [email removed].


Employment Information

Employment is contingent upon verification of eligibility to work in the United States (E-Verify).

RGS & AWS is an equal opportunity employer. All qualified applicants will receive consideration without regard to race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, national origin, age, disability, veteran status, or any other protected status under applicable law.

Hours per Week: 35 – 40 
Cost: $289USD/Week  
  Description: 
 The T.R.E.E.S Farm has been established as a Farm-to-Table organic operation and regenerative agriculture demonstration farm. Its primary purpose is to serve the original needs of the NGO’s operations which are wildlife conservation through research and education. This is accomplished through the layout of the farm which provides extensive wildlife habitat and foraging opportunities, increasing the local faunal biodiversity as well as acting as an educational demonstration to local subsistence farmers and visiting students.  
  Interns will learn by assisting in implementation and evaluation of management practices, cropping, and record keeping on the farm with this vision in mind while we endeavor to maximize the products coming from the farm with the existing design and layout using sustainable and regenerative practices specific to the Mesoamerican uplands. Within this broad framework, intern projects can include several basic Agricultural Education disciplines including Tropical Agriculture, Sustainable/organic Agriculture, Farm Management, Waste management, and Agricultural Economics.  
  In addition to planting crops, we also have free range chickens and ducks for eggs and meat. We are looking to increase our revenue generation from the farm either in the form of increased accountable products entering our kitchen for use in our restaurant, or for sale to the Mobile Market or in a proposed road-side café which would be managed by T.R.E.E.S kitchen and hospitality staff. Thus, interns would also assist us with our marketing strategy for existing products and/or planting. 
  By the successful conclusion of this internship, the student will be able to apply practical methods for planting and maintaining various typical and exotic tropical crop species, basic free range poultry operations, evaluate different treatments using objective measurements of biomass, yield, and costs/returns, and become familiar with sustainable management practices such as no/low till, cover cropping, waste management, mulching, marketing, Farm-to-Table, etc. 
    Requirements: 
 No prior tropical agriculture experience required. Interns can be current undergraduate or graduate students enrolled in a program with their University/College for credit, however non-students can also apply; but preference will be given to students enrolled in an accreditation program. Experienced tropical agriculturalists and/or agroforestry professionals are also welcome and will be treated according to their experience level and are eligible for *discounted rates. 
    Internship Responsibilities: 
 Applying practical methods for planting and maintaining various typical and exotic tropical crop species and basic free range poultry operations. 
Evaluating different treatments using objective measurements of biomass, yield, and costs/returns. 
Work on Inga Alley-cropping and other regenerative cropping practices, and using intercropping, organic fertilizing and pest control practices. 
Assist with innovative marketing strategies for existing products accompanied by reviewing projected budgets for the farm and their products and exploring cost/profit ratios for poultry husbandry. 
Planting and selling new products for the farm. 
Opportunities are also available to observe and participate with concurrent intern and wildlife educational activities such as mist-netting, observing and recording measurements of bats, birds, herps, invertebrates, water quality, and much more. 
Interns will assist with creating captions for social media posts to engage and update followers on what has been going on at the field station and various projects that are being done. 
     Costs: 
 The internship fee includes room and board, full access to lab equipment, and training by professional on-site biologists. Food is a combination of self-catering in a communal kitchen with ingredients provided as well as prepared meals, depending on whether we have other groups on site. Lodging at the research center signifies a shared dormitory-style rustic cabins with other same sex interns. This comes with full access to other facilities such as showers, restrooms, and kitchen. The nature of this program allows interns to carry out most of the work independently after the training period is done. Fees do not include airport transfer, flights, travel medical insurance, or $100 USD visitor permit fee if remaining in country for more than 30 days.    
  We are hoping to expand our internship program beyond North America. Citizens from Latin America and the Caribbean will be charged at a discounted rate of 50%. Belizeans will get another discount. For more information, kindly email Scandia Cruz with the email provided above. 
    Schedule: 
 Interns are required to work for 35 hours/week minimum. The typical schedule runs from Monday through Friday, from 6:30 am until 12:30 pm and 3:30 pm to 5:30 pm. Weekends are free time for interns; therefore, you can do as please (travel, hike, relax). No refunds on food and lodging will be available if the intern decides to leave the station. Projects may sometimes run into the weekend; in which case the days will be returned to them during the week. The intern supervisor(s) will be responsible for designing a schedule with the intern each week that is reasonable and includes work on the various projects.

 For more information on our organization and facilities please visit our website: www.treesociety.org. To apply, please visit ecorana.ca/apply. For any questions, please contact [email removed].

Position Description
 WRFI is currently seeking an instructor with deep experience in the visual arts to co-lead the Southwest Climate Studio Art course for 2027 and beyond. The course curriculum was collaboratively developed with several existing WRFI instructors and leadership staff to serve a population of undergraduate students studying the visual arts who traditionally do not have access to academic field experiences. Several of the original course designers have moved on from WRFI, and we are now seeking an instructor who is interested in teaching from the existing curriculum, collaborating with other instructors, and taking a leadership role in developing the course content and curriculum, particularly in the visual arts.

Who We Are:  The Wild Rockies Field Institute offers academically rigorous, place-based field courses that develop engaged, informed citizens and strong leaders capable of addressing complex social and environmental issues. We offer college students the opportunity to study ecology, public lands issues, rural development, philosophy, and cultural history during extended backcountry expeditions and visits to rural communities in the Rocky Mountain West. 
 Job Title, Location, and Supervisor: Field Instructors work in a field-based setting to facilitate WRFI courses.  This position reports to the Field Education Manager.  This role is contract-based, short term, and temporary, and therefore not eligible for benefits.

Job Objective: Field Instructors develop and execute WRFI’s academic field programs, leading undergraduate students in outdoor settings throughout the American and Canadian Rockies.
 Job Qualifications: The successful candidate must have excellent communication and computer skills; the ability to work well with the public, students, other field instructors, and office staff; keen attention to detail; a capacity to work independently; and the desire to participate in a variety of tasks. The successful candidate will be experienced in outdoor education programming, operations, logistics, and staffing, experienced delivering collegiate-level academics, committed to diversity, equity, and inclusion work, and an experienced risk manager. Additionally, the ideal candidate will be familiar with Google platforms. A master’s degree in the visual arts is required due to requirements for instruction through the University of Montana. A current WFR or higher certification is required prior to instructing in the field.
 Compensation: Field Instructors are paid according to a pay table, both for hourly and daily work.  WRFI’s most updated pay table is viewable here.

Equal Opportunity: Wild Rockies Field Institute is an equal opportunity organization and does not and shall not discriminate on the basis of race, color, religion, gender identity or expression, age, national origin (ancestry), disability, marital status, sexual orientation, spousal affiliation, mental or physical disability, serious medical condition, or military status in any of its activities or operations. WRFI recognizes that access to environmental education—along with access to nature spaces, clean air and water, and healthy food—continues to be a privilege. WRFI additionally recognizes that in outdoor and environmental education organizations, the voices and work of people of color, people from low income backgrounds, unhoused people, Indigenous people, women, and LGBTQ2S+ individuals have been often overlooked and/or intentionally marginalized. Therefore, we especially encourage applications from people who identify in these groups.

Unique Aspects of Instruction on Southwest Climate Studio Art:
The Southwest Climate Studio Art curriculum bridges a unique space between climate change studies and climate communication as well as visual arts in an upper division setting. The curriculum includes two classes: Climate Change Studies CCS 391 - Community-Based Resilience to Climate Change and Studio Art ARTZ 395 - Cultural Climate Expression in the American Southwest which are taught concurrently and collaboratively. WRFI seeks an instructor with an MFA in visual arts to lead the instruction of the art curriculum of this program. 
The expectation students bring to this course is an opportunity to explore Spanish and Indigenous artistic and agricultural traditions/practices in the American Southwest while also developing their own artistic practices to represent an experience of a changing climate today. In order to facilitate this course, an instructor must be comfortable with numerous visits to local experts in the Southwest, including Indigenous and Spanish agricultural leaders, artists, scientists, and community leaders. The SCSA curriculum focuses on two topics: climate change studies, specifically through a lens of human resilience; and visual arts and building a studio practice. A collaborative teaching approach with local experts is critical to building a course curriculum that is coherent, place-based, and impactful for students on the course. WRFI seeks an instructor who is comfortable and committed to teaching these topics through these experiential learning practices.

 While this course is fully a "frontcountry" program (vehicle supported), we do require instructors to have a WFR certification, extensive outdoor experience, and comfort and familiarity with leading a group of undergraduate students while camping and living outdoors for the duration of the course. At times, the course will stay in remote, off-grid, dry camping areas without running water, established campsites, or restroom facilities. Additionally, while having an interest in climate change science is encouraged, this instructor will work closely with a co-instructor with a background/expertise in climate change science. We are seeking an instructor comfortable with being the expert in the room when it comes to visual arts who is excited about collaboration with a climate science expert on overall curriculum goals.

Job Responsibilities:

WRFI Field Instructors hold the ultimate responsibility for all happenings while on course, including experiential, academic, and technical.  This means that Instructors must:

Adhere to the WRFI Code of Ethics (see below)
Adhere to WRFI Risk Management and Safety Policies (see below)
Accept full responsibility for the course they arranged to co-instruct, demonstrated by clear communication with office staff and fellow instructors, a consistently professional attitude, and a teamwork mentality.
Complete Pre-Course work, including:
Participation in at least three 90-minute pre-course briefing meetings in the 120 days prior to each course’s launch date
Participation in creating course materials for students (equipment list, syllabus, itinerary, reader, course assignments, etc);
Maintain and update shared course electronic files;
Obtain and organize necessary gear and food;
Participation in creating and submitting course reader and course packet;
Obtaining additional curriculum materials as needed;
Arrange guest speakers;
Arrange front-country camping/lodging;
Submit an itinerary to the WRFI office, including marked call-in days and a general outline of daily educational activities/assignments;
Update course-specific emergency contact list and evacuation plans.

Complete Post-Course work, including:
Complete course accounting sheets, including all receipts and remaining petty cash within 30 days of the end of your section and/or the course end;
Update the course itinerary document with actual use (including permitted use days) and actual itinerary within 30 days of course completion
Complete self and co-instructor evaluations;
Write student letters;
Write parent letters;
Complete grading and submit grades to WRFI within three weeks of course end and make copies of grade sheets for WRFI files;
Label and submit photos to Google Photos, including at least one close-up group shot and one portrait of each student (if possible);
Write and send thank you notes to all guest speakers;
Clean and return gear at end of course (make repairs, mark for warranty, or replace as needed);
Restock First Aid Kit;
Update course documents (including bibliography, syllabus, gear list, itinerary, reading list, and website text recommendations) within 30 days of course end;
Participate in course debrief with Office staff and other instructors.

WRFI Instructor Code of Ethics
 The safety of all individuals on the course must be the primary focus of all WRFI instructors.
Because WRFI is an educational institution, it holds students to rigorous academic performance standards. Grades awarded to WRFI students reflect only the student’s academic performance during the course. They do not reflect the personality or an assumed personal worth of the student.
WRFI instructors are expected to refrain from any inappropriately personal or sexual liaison with any student or intern. No form of sexual harassment will be tolerated.
Instructors are expected to maintain a focus on the safety and education of the entire group, regardless of personalities or interpersonal relationships.
Instructors must obey all the laws and regulations of the jurisdictions in which the course takes place.
Negative environmental and social impacts should be minimized where possible, both in the course area, and during course preparation.
Wild Rockies Field Institute is an equal opportunity organization and does not and shall not discriminate on the basis of race, color, religion, gender identity or expression, age, national origin (ancestry), disability, marital status, sexual orientation, spousal affiliation, mental or physical disability, serious medical condition, or military status in any of its activities or operations. Any acts of harassment, threats of violence, intolerance, or discrimination are grounds for immediate dismissal.

WRFI Safety Policy
 Statement of Principle
This section provides an overview of WRFI Safety Policies. Instructors must follow more specific safety policies and guidelines specific to course activities and locations as detailed in the most recent Risk Management and Safety Manual. WRFI will provide these manuals to each instructor.
 Each instructor directly, and WRFI overall, is responsible for the safety of each student while the course is in session.
Instructors must have a written emergency procedure that includes:
an evacuation plan;
maps showing details of routes used ;
phone lists of local emergency agencies and the WRFI emergency phone-in procedure;
policies and procedures for dealing  with a major injury and/or fatality;
incident report forms ;
contact WRFI office for any incident resulting in a student leaving the field.
Instructors must review and carry a copy of all staff and student medical forms.
Instructors must carry complete WRFI First Aid Kits.
Instructors must provide a safety briefing for students before each activity that includes:
the general emergency plan including instructor, intern, and student roles and responsibilities;
a warning of the difficulty of evacuation and the need for caution;
a description of known and potential environmental hazards;
instruction on appropriate equipment use including stoves, boats, vans and trailers;
See pre-course checklist for more detail on topics to be covered.
Instructors are responsible to have and maintain all necessary safety equipment
Instructors will inspect equipment for proper function and safety prior to student use.
Possession or use of alcohol and illegal drugs is expressly prohibited during all courses.
Instructors are responsible for communicating behaviors that in their judgment unduly compromises the safety of the group or the educational value of the course to the WRFI office to make a plan, up to and including removal of a student from the course.

Job Summary
The Department of Natural Resources is seeking one (1) NR Specialist Senior – Wildlife Research to support the Farmland Wildlife Populations and Research Group, based in Madelia, MN. This position assists the Ungulate Research Scientist, who provides overall direction for the group’s ungulate research and monitoring program. This position exists: (1) to plan, conduct, analyze, and report on studies of white-tailed deer and elk, both independently and under direction from the Research Scientist on statewide research and monitoring programs; (2) to develop, evaluate, and implement new techniques for assessing, monitoring, and managing ungulate populations and their resources; (3) to disseminate advanced technical expertise to Wildlife staff, other natural resource professionals, and the public; and (4) to represent the Department in public. 

Responsibilities include but are not limited to:

Perform all job responsibilities in a manner that supports a healthy, safe, and productive work environment for all employees. Encourage a diverse workplace, treat others with respect, and contribute to work groups. Support the overall mission of the Department.
To identify information needs and to plan and design original research and survey projects (e.g., population monitoring) in collaboration with the Research Scientist on the ecology and management of farmland ungulates, to meet needs for increased scientific knowledge, improved technology, and improved management of Minnesota’s farmland game resources. 
To organize and conduct research activities and surveys (including topics related to ungulate survival and cause-specific mortality, habitat and predator interactions, and population monitoring and dynamics), working both independently and in conjunction with the Research Scientist, using appropriate techniques so study objectives are met and findings are statistically and scientifically valid.
To analyze data and interpret research results so valid inferences can be made and appropriate conclusions can be drawn.
Provide technical assistance and report results and conclusions of research and survey projects in oral and written format so that findings can be used by scientists, natural resource managers, administrators, and the public within Minnesota, the U.S., and internationally.
To remain current in knowledge, technologies, and peer collaborations so that the most modern scientific understanding and practices are used to conduct research. Develop or apply advanced, state-of-the-art techniques and technologies to evaluate defined problems.

This position requires the incumbent to work in adverse weather and environmental conditions such as heat, rain/humidity, extreme cold, and being exposed to ticks and biting insects. The incumbent must be air-worthy and able to conduct aerial telemetry and/or surveys from small fixed-wing or rotary aircraft. This position has a flexible work arrangement and may be eligible to telework on a part-time basis, which is subject to change. If approved, the employee would be required to complete an annual telework agreement. This position will require reporting to the primary work location on a regular basis.

Minimum Qualifications
A master's degree (thesis) in wildlife ecology or closely related field, and two (2) years of professional (post-graduation) wildlife research experience; or a PhD in wildlife ecology or closely related field.
Knowledge of wildlife ecology, management, and conservation of Minnesota ungulates and their predators.
Experience designing, implementing, analyzing, interpreting, and reporting management-oriented wildlife research.
Experience with many phases of field work including:
Developing fieldwork protocols, including ungulate capture and monitoring protocols. 
Safely capturing, handling, and immobilizing ungulates. 
Tracking wildlife using radiotelemetry or GPS (including triangulation and homing techniques), collar testing, and responding to mortality events.
Vegetation/habitat sampling.
Experience leading the work of others.
Knowledge of statistics sufficient to interpret and analyze ecological data properly.
Experience with ArcPro and Program R, or equivalent statistical software.
Computer proficiency, including knowledge of databases, spreadsheets, and statistical programs sufficient to manage data input, retrieval and compilation, maintain databases, and train others to use these systems.
Communication skills sufficient to maintain exemplary relationships with Minnesota wildlife managers and answer relevant research questions. 
Experience communicating with diverse audiences, including both public and peer groups, sufficient to document and disseminate completed research results. 
Ability to work effectively and courteously with people and navigate controversial topics in a professional and respectful manner.
Experience preparing final reports, including authoring and publishing of peer-reviewed scientific journal articles. 
Ability to safely operate a variety of equipment, including 4-wheel-drive pick-ups, winches, snowmobiles, ATV/UTVs and trailers, in challenging field conditions.

Preferred Qualifications
Ph.D. in wildlife ecology or a closely related area. 
Research experience with ungulates, particularly field-based research with white-tailed deer or elk. 
Experience directly related to the publication of research results in the peer-reviewed scientific literature, including at least two (2) manuscripts in review, in press, or previously published in a wildlife management-oriented or applied focus journal.
Experience designing and/or conducting population monitoring surveys (e.g., camera trap surveys, distance sampling surveys, and/or aerial surveys).
Experience conducting surveys and aerial telemetry from fixed wing aircraft and/or helicopters.
Experience estimating parameters (e.g., survival, trends) of animal populations.
Proficiency conducting statistical analysis of wildlife data using Program R and ArcPro.
Experience conducting wildlife habitat use analyses (e.g., home range, step selection function, etc.). 

Additional Requirements
This position requires an unrestricted Class D Driver’s License with a clear driving record. Per DNR Fleet Policy, only individuals 18 years of age or older with a valid driver’s license may operate equipment and vehicles on behalf of the Agency.

We encourage you to apply, even if you don't believe you meet every one of our described qualifications or have a less traditional background. We are looking for applicants with the following:

 Experience: 
·       Minimum of seven years professional experience in policy development and advocacy.
·       Development and presentation of written and oral testimony.
·       Preparation of white papers, reports, and articles for professional and lay audiences.
·       Budget development and tracking. 
·       Project and grant management. 
·       Volunteer recruitment, training, management, and motivation.

·       Effective and respectful verbal and written communication skills.

MSU Marine Fisheries Ecology Program 2027 Internship
 The Mississippi State University Marine Fisheries Ecology Program (https://msucoastal.com/marine-fisheries/) is seeking applicants for an internship position working under the direction of Dr. Marcus Drymon and Extension Associates at the Coastal Research and Extension Center (CREC) in Biloxi, MS.  The roles of the intern will fall into three categories: field, laboratory, and outreach/education. The first category involves assisting with shark bottom longline surveys throughout the northern Gulf of Mexico. Specifically, the intern will be responsible for preparing gear, performing shark and fish dissections, collecting samples, and recording and entering data. The second category involves completing various laboratory processing tasks using samples collected during the bottom longline surveys. The third category involves helping with outreach and education events and developing materials to use at these events. Travel for field work and outreach events may be necessary.

B.S. or B.A. in biological sciences (must be graduated by March 2027).

Ability to speak with outside groups, particularly in an education setting.

Description
Two Postdoctoral Positions in Human Dimensions of Deer and CWD Management

Purdue University and Michigan State University | Joint recruitment announcement
Interested in working on a dynamic and interdisciplinary team that integrates human dimensions, ecology and epidemiology…and want your research to have real-world impacts?

Purdue University and Michigan State University (MSU) are each recruiting a postdoctoral researcher for in-person positions at their respective universities, supporting a multistate deer and chronic wasting disease (CWD) management project.

The Multistate Project
This multistate adaptive management project was developed through the CWD Research Consortium in partnership with state wildlife agencies, universities, and federal research collaborators. The project tests whether coordinated, community-based behavioral interventions can increase antlerless deer harvest and improve deer population and CWD management outcomes, using paired treatment and control units across participating
Midwestern states. It combines assessments of landowner social and behavioral conditions and responses to interventions with monitoring of deer harvest, density, demographics, and CWD prevalence.

Human dimensions research examines factors influencing landowner decisions about deer harvest, participation in management activities, and responses to behavioral
interventions, using the findings to inform intervention design.

Research Team
The research team includes Dr. Zhao Ma (human dimensions) of Purdue University; Dr. Emily Pomeranz (human dimensions) at Michigan State University; Dr. Daniel Walsh
(statistics and disease ecology), Maggie Johnson (disease ecology), Dr. Kaylin Clements (human dimensions), and Dr. Alex Metcalf (human dimensions) of the University of
Montana; Dr. Megan Jones (communication science) of Oregon State University, along with other human dimensions scientists, ecologists and epidemiologists from USGS, USDA, and state wildlife agencies.

Both postdoctoral researchers will collaboratively develop and refine survey instruments, coordinate methods, and develop and evaluate behavioral interventions. This collaboration will support standardized data collection and analyses within participating states and across the region.

Purdue University position
Based in West Lafayette, Indiana, the postdoc will be supervised by Dr. Zhao Ma at Purdue University and Dr. Daniel Walsh at the University of Montana. Building on ongoing qualitative pilot research, the postdoc will help design and refine a quantitative landowner survey and lead its implementation, data management, and analysis in Ohio and Missouri. This includes coordinating sampling and questionnaire pretesting with agency partners, preparing materials for institutional review board review, and coordinating human subjects research requirements.

The postdoc will work with the Michigan State University postdoc and the CWD Research Consortium team to align survey methods, analyze data across states, and help coordinate human dimensions research across Ohio, Michigan, and Missouri. The postdoc will use findings to help develop and evaluate interventions aimed at increasing antlerless harvest and contribute to formative evaluation of the project. Other duties include contributing to a systematic literature review and qualitative research with landowners as needed, sharing progress and findings with project partners and agency leadership, and contributing to manuscripts, presentations, and agency reports. For more detail on the Purdue position, please visit https://www.purdue.edu/fnr/sites/ma/opportunities/.

The postdoc will join Purdue’s Human Dimensions Lab, where students, postdoctoral researchers, and staff study the human dimensions of natural resources and global
change. Projects range from deer management and forest restoration to community science and incentive-based conservation. The lab uses mixed methods and works across disciplines to inform natural resource management and address community partners’ priorities.

Michigan State University position
Based in East Lansing, Michigan, the postdoc will be supervised by Dr. Emily Pomeranz in Michigan State University’s Department of Fisheries and Wildlife and work closely with Michigan Department of Natural Resources partners. The postdoc will help design and refine a quantitative landowner survey and lead its implementation, data management, and analysis in Michigan. This includes coordinating sampling, questionnaire pretesting, and human subjects research requirements.

The postdoc will work with the Purdue postdoc and the CWD Research Consortium team to align survey methods and analyze data across states. The postdoc will use findings to help develop and evaluate interventions aimed at increasing antlerless harvest and contribute to formative evaluation of the Michigan project. Other duties include engaging with stakeholders, mentoring graduate students, and contributing to manuscripts and presentations. Qualitative research with landowners may complement the survey work as project needs and time allow.

The postdoctoral research associate will join Dr. Emily Pomeranz’s research group in Michigan State University’s Department of Fisheries and Wildlife. The group studies how people participate in wildlife conservation decisions and how their beliefs, attitudes, and behaviors shape wildlife management. Working closely with Michigan DNR Wildlife Division and other research and agency partners, the group conducts applied research on stakeholder engagement, public participation, and community-based wildlife management. For more details on the MSU position please visit: MSU Link.

Appointment details
Both positions are in person and have a preferred start date of January 1, 2027. A later start date may be considered.

Purdue University: This is a full-time position based in West Lafayette, Indiana. USDA APHIS funding is available for one year, with the possibility of a one-year extension contingent on performance and funding availability.

Michigan State University: This position is based in East Lansing, Michigan, and is funded for at least two years. The postdoc will support a four-year project led by Michigan State University in partnership with the Michigan Department of Natural Resources.

Qualifications
Applicants must have a Ph.D. in conservation social science, human dimensions of natural resources, or a related field by the start date. Both positions call for experience designing and implementing quantitative surveys, strong quantitative analysis skills, and the ability to communicate research clearly to scientific and management audiences. Applicants should be able to organize research activities and work effectively with interdisciplinary research teams and agency partners.
The Purdue position also requires a valid U.S. driver’s license. See the individual postings for the full required and preferred qualifications for each position.

How to apply
If either opportunity interests you, we encourage you to apply for both positions. Purdue University and Michigan State University review applications independently. Each
application is considered only for the position to which it was submitted, so please follow each university’s application instructions if you’d like to be considered for both.

Apply to Purdue University
Please submit the following in a single PDF file to Dr. Zhao Ma ([email removed]) via email: (1) cover letter describing your relevant experience and scholarly interests; (2) curriculum vitae; (3) two examples of relevant publications or writing samples; and (4) contact information of three references. Please use the following subject for your email “Postdoc_Deer_Last Name.” Review of applications will start on December 1, 2026 and will continue until the position is filled. Purdue is an equal opportunity affirmative action employer. For more information, contact Dr. Zhao Ma. Detailed posting found here: https://www.purdue.edu/fnr/sites/ma/opportunities/

Apply to Michigan State University
Apply at http://careers.msu.edu under job number [1179364; or follow this link: MSU Link. Required materials are a cover letter of no more than two pages, curriculum vitae, and names and contact information for three professional references. Review begins December 1st, 2026, and continues until a suitable candidate is selected. Questions: Dr. Emily Pomeranz, [email removed]
Contact
Emily Pomeranz (MSU) & Zhao Ma (Purdue)

Title: Aquarist / Marine Science Educator Internship housing and utilities included 

Organization: Gulf Specimen Marine Lab 

Location: Panacea, Florida 

Time Period of Position: Starting in early March 2026 and ending about the end of August 2027. 

Gulf Specimen Marine Lab and Aquarium is a nonprofit with a mission of educating the public about our oceans to create good stewards of our ocean ecosystems. We are a public aquarium open almost every day of the year with thousands of gallons of saltwater aquarium displays. Organisms on display include sea turtles, stingrays, sharks, octopus, a large touch tank room, and more. GSML is also a marine life educational facility with thousands of guests visiting for guided tours each year. For over fifty years, we have functioned as a biological supply to universities and aquariums, supplying live organisms for research and education purposes only. We are also one of the oldest sea turtle hospital/ rehabilitation facilities in operation. 
 We are looking to fill three positions for six-month internships with housing and utilities provided. These are unpaid positions. We provide housing with utilities. There is no other compensation or stipend provided. 
 Job Description: The Aquarist / Marine Science Educator Internship is like on-the-job training. You will perform duties in all four areas of our operations, which include the public aquarium, marine life educational tours, biological supply, and sea turtle rescue and rehab. 
Public aquarium duties include cleaning aquarium displays, feeding organisms, treating organisms, keeping dry displays neat and clean, fixing plumbing issues, and helping to construct new displays. Helping in the gift shop and front office by ringing up guests' purchases. Covering the office and answering phone calls for orders when the office staff are out or on break. Managing social media accounts for the aquarium. Creating content and posting regularly to the aquarium's social media. Helping with periodic special events such as marine life educational summer camps and special themed events at the aquarium. At a public aquarium, everything that the public can see is part of the display and needs to be neat, clean, orderly, and professional-looking. All the areas behind the scenes need to be neat, clean, orderly, and professional-looking to function. If you do not agree with the statement “if a task needs doing, it is in my job description,” please do not apply for this internship. 
Our marine life educational programs involve conducting marine life educational tours. You will need to be comfortable with public speaking. We offer three tours at our facility, which include a one-hour aquarium tour, a two-hour tour of the aquarium and dock, and a three-hour tour of the aquarium, dock, and marsh. We also operate a traveling exhibit. Going along and a few trips with the traveling exhibit will also be part of the internship. 
The biological supply duties will include trips out on our collecting boats to collect the biological specimens. Transporting the organisms back to the aquarium and acclimating them. Helping to pack orders to be shipped to universities and aquariums for educational purposes. 
The sea turtle rescue and rehabilitation duties include responding to calls for sick or injured sea turtles. Assisting in performing recommended treatments, gathering measurement data for forms, feeding and caring for sick or injured turtles. 
A successful intern will be able to live and work well with people of various backgrounds in a small-work environment. The ability to separate personal issues from professional time (and the ability to resolve any personal issues quickly with little conflict) is crucial to this position. A good attitude and work ethic are very important. 
 A little information about the area: Gulf Specimen Marine Lab is located in Panacea, Florida, which is in an area known as the Nature Coast. It is largely undeveloped along the coast compared to other areas of Florida. It is a biodiversity hotspot, meaning a wide variety of organisms can be found in the area both in the ocean and on the land. There is a lot to do and see involving nature. If you love nature, especially the ocean, it will be a nice location for you. Interns will live in housing on site right next to the marine lab where you will work and across the street from the bay. 
 Qualifications: Graduate of a degree program in marine biology, marine conservation, marine aquarist or a related field. Your degree program must have included a variety of classes in and related to marine biology. A high level of interest (experience preferred) in marine life aquarium husbandry and/or teaching students of diverse ages and backgrounds about conservation of and information on marine organisms and ecosystems. Excellent public speaking skills for audiences of various ages and abilities. An optimistic, “can-do” attitude. Willingness to clean aquariums and displays and keep the facility looking beautiful. The ability to work independently and in a team setting while foreseeing and quickly correcting potential problems. The ability to work well with others in a small organization where your coworkers are also your roommates. Experience with Microsoft Office, Google Drive, and various social media formats preferred but not required.
 Housing: Housing is provided on site right next to the marine lab and across the street from the bay. A three-bedroom apartment that will be shared by the three interns. The apartment is fully furnished and includes everything needed to cook. The apartment has three bedrooms and a common area, which includes the living room, kitchen, and full bathroom. Utilities are included, which are electricity, water, and internet. There is a laundry area on site where interns can use it for free with their own supplies.
